title: Number of Steps to Reduce a Number to Zero

content.title: Number of Steps to Reduce a Number to Zero

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given a non-negative number, count how many steps it takes to bring it down to zero, halving it when even and subtracting 1 when odd.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.text: Given a non-negative number num, count how many steps it takes to bring it down to zero. On every step, if the current number is even, divide it by 2. If it is odd, subtract 1 from it.

blocks.title: Analogy: The Staircase That Halves or Drops
blocks.text: Picture a staircase where every step down works one of two ways. If you are standing on an even numbered stair, a trapdoor drops you straight down to half that height. If you are standing on an odd numbered stair, there is no trapdoor, you simply step down by one onto the stair below, which is always even, so the very next move is guaranteed to be a halving drop. The question is just counting how many of these moves it takes to reach the ground floor.

blocks.caption: The only two moves available at any step

blocks.text: The number is already at zero. No operation is needed at all, so the answer is simply 0 steps. This is the edge case worth checking directly.
Before writing any code, it helps to reason about what these two operations actually do to the number's binary form.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Every even number gets halved, which is exactly the same as shifting its binary representation one position to the right.

Observation 2: Every odd number gets exactly 1 subtracted, which only ever clears its lowest bit, turning it from 1 to 0, and that always makes the result even.

Observation 3: So the total number of divide steps is really just how many bit positions the number has, and the total number of subtract steps is really just how many of those bit positions are 1.

Observation 4: If both of those counts can be read directly from the binary representation, there is no need to simulate the process at all.
That reasoning alone already points at the shortcut: the answer is just bit length and popcount, combined with one formula.

The most direct approach is to literally simulate the process: repeatedly check whether the current number is even or odd, apply the matching operation, and count every operation performed, until the number reaches zero.

items: Start a counter at 0.
While num is greater than 0, check whether it is even or odd.
If even, divide num by 2. If odd, subtract 1 from num.
Increase the counter by 1 for that operation, and repeat.
Return the counter once num reaches 0.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: simulate one operation at a time

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The even/odd check happens first inside the loop, before any modification, since which operation applies depends entirely on num's current parity at that exact moment.
steps is incremented exactly once per loop iteration, regardless of whether that iteration divided or subtracted, since the problem counts both kinds of operations equally.
The loop condition checks num > 0 rather than num != 0, a small defensive habit, though for this problem's guaranteed non-negative input the two behave identically.

blocks.text: This works because it directly follows the two rules given in the problem, one operation at a time, until nothing is left.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(log num). Every odd step is immediately followed by an even step, since subtracting 1 from an odd number always makes it even, so the number roughly halves every one or two steps.
Space: O(1), just a counter and the number itself.

Limitation: even though this is already efficient, it does real arithmetic work and a branch on every single step. The final answer actually only depends on two simple facts about num's binary representation: how many bits it has, and how many of those bits are 1s, neither of which requires simulating the subtract-and-divide process at all.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why simulating every step works but is not necessary: each individual operation is cheap, but the total count can be read from the number's structure instead of walking through every operation.

What the operations actually correspond to: dividing by 2 shifts the binary representation right by one bit, and subtracting 1 from an odd number clears its lowest bit.

Can the total divide count be found without simulating: yes, it equals the number's bit length, since every bit position gets shifted through exactly once.

Can the total subtract count be found without simulating: yes, it equals the number's popcount, since every 1-bit requires exactly one subtract to clear it.

The core idea: read bit length and popcount directly, combine them with one formula, no simulation needed.

Every divide-by-2 step corresponds to moving one bit position to the right in num's binary form, so the total number of divide steps equals num's bit length minus one. Every odd step, a subtract, happens exactly once for every 1-bit in that binary form, because a 1-bit is what makes a number odd at that stage.
The optimization is to read those two counts, bit length and count of 1-bits, directly from num's binary representation, and combine them with a formula instead of simulating anything.

Count the total number of bits in num (its bit length) and the total number of 1-bits (its popcount) in a single pass. The answer is (bit length minus 1) plus popcount, one divide for every bit position but the last, plus one subtract for every 1-bit.

blocks.content: {"headers":["temp (binary)","bitLength after","popcount after","Why"],"rows":[["14 (1110)","1","0","Lowest bit is 0, so this position contributes to bit length but not popcount."],["7 (111)","2","1","Lowest bit is now 1, popcount increases."],["3 (11)","3","2","Lowest bit is 1 again, popcount increases again."],["1 (1)","4","3","Final bit position, also a 1, popcount reaches its final value."]]}

blocks.text: Final bitLength is 4 and popcount is 3, giving (4 minus 1) plus 3 = 6, matching the step by step simulation exactly.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: read the answer off the bits directly

codes.python:
def number_of_steps(num):
    if num == 0:
        return 0                  # already at zero, no steps needed
    bit_length = 0                # total number of bits in num's binary form
    popcount = 0                  # count of 1-bits, each needs one extra subtract step
    temp = num
    while temp > 0:
        bit_length += 1            # one more bit position seen
        popcount += temp & 1       # check if the lowest bit is a 1
        temp >>= 1                  # move to the next bit
    return (bit_length - 1) + popcount  # one divide per bit position minus the last, plus a subtract per 1-bit


if __name__ == "__main__":
    num = 14
    print(number_of_steps(num))

blocks.text: This works because every divide-by-2 operation is mathematically identical to a right shift of the binary representation, and that shift happens exactly once per bit position, giving bit length minus 1 total shifts. Every subtract-by-1 operation clears exactly one 1-bit, and there is exactly one such operation per 1-bit in the entire number, giving popcount total subtracts. Adding these two independently derived counts together gives the exact same total the simulation would have counted one operation at a time.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What It Counts","Why"],"rows":[["bit length minus 1","Every divide-by-2 step, one per bit position except the very last","Shifting right happens once per bit position, and after bit length minus 1 shifts, only the final subtract-or-nothing check remains."],["popcount","Every subtract-by-1 step, one per 1-bit","Each 1-bit needs exactly one subtract to turn it into a 0, since a 1-bit is what makes that intermediate value odd."]]}

items: The while loop shifts temp right one bit at a time purely to discover bitLength and popcount, it never touches or returns temp itself, num stays completely untouched.
popcount += temp & 1 adds either 0 or 1 on every iteration, checking only the single lowest bit each time, which is exactly what & 1 isolates.
The num == 0 check happens before the loop as a dedicated early return, since the main loop would otherwise just skip everything and silently return 0 anyway, but making it explicit reads clearer.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(log num), one pass over the bits, the same order as the simulation but with no branching arithmetic on num itself.
Space: O(1), just two counters.

Both bit length and popcount can be computed with a manual loop, as shown above, or read out using built-in functions that most languages expose, several of which map directly to a single CPU instruction rather than a software loop.

Intuition: counting bits is such a common operation that modern processors include a dedicated POPCNT instruction for it. Using the language's built-in bit length and popcount functions instead of a manual loop lets the runtime take advantage of that hardware support directly.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Call","Result","Why"],"rows":[["bit length of 14","4","Same value the manual loop computed, now read directly from a built-in function."],["popcount of 14","3","Same value the manual loop computed, now read directly from a hardware instruction."],["steps = (4 minus 1) plus 3","6","The exact same formula as the manual version, only its two inputs changed how they were obtained."]]}

blocks.caption: Further optimization: hand the bit counting off to built-in hardware support

items: The bit length built-in computes the exact same "how many bit positions does this number occupy" value the manual loop computed, just using a language or compiler built-in instead of a hand written loop.
The popcount built-in similarly replaces the manual popcount loop, and on most modern CPUs compiles down to a single hardware POPCNT instruction.
The formula itself, (bitLength minus 1) plus popcount, is completely unchanged from the manual version, only how the two inputs to that formula are obtained has changed.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(log num) in the worst theoretical case, but effectively a small constant number of hardware instructions in practice.
Space: O(1), identical to the manual version, this is purely a constant-factor and implementation improvement.

blocks.text: The core pattern here is recognizing that a step by step simulation is secretly counting properties of a number's binary representation: the number of divide steps is the bit length, and the number of subtract steps is the population count of 1-bits. Once that connection is made, no simulation is needed at all.

items: Forgetting the num = 0 edge case, which needs 0 steps and no computation.
Off by one errors between bit length and the number of divide operations, remember it is bit length minus one, not bit length itself.
Assuming a bigger number always means proportionally more steps, when what actually matters is the number of 1-bits, not the number's size alone.

blocks.text: This problem rewards noticing the connection between a simulation and the underlying binary representation, rather than stopping at the first working loop. Mentioning that the final answer is just bit length and popcount, and that many languages expose hardware accelerated built-ins for both, signals a stronger grasp of what the computer is actually doing under the hood.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid simulating every step", think: the answer is just bit length minus 1 plus popcount.
If the interviewer says "can you use built-in functions", think: most languages expose a hardware accelerated popcount and bit length function directly.
If the interviewer says "why does every odd step get followed by an even step", think: subtracting 1 from an odd number always clears its lowest bit, which always makes the result even.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: All three approaches run in O(log num) time and O(1) space. The differences are entirely about how that work gets done: a branching simulation, a manual bit counting pass, or handing the counting off to built-in hardware support, each faster in practice than the last without changing the underlying complexity class.

items: Pattern: a step by step simulation that secretly counts two properties of the number's binary representation, bit length and popcount.

Core Idea: every divide-by-2 step corresponds to one bit position (bit length minus 1 total), and every subtract-by-1 step corresponds to one 1-bit (popcount total); adding them gives the answer directly.
Time: O(log num) for every version shown here.
Space: O(1) for every version shown here.

Most Important Observation: the operations described in the problem are literally how binary shifting and bit clearing work, so the simulation and the direct formula are two descriptions of the exact same underlying process.
Interview Difficulty: easy to simulate correctly, but spotting the bit length plus popcount shortcut, and knowing built-ins exist for both, is what makes an answer stand out.
One line memory trick: steps equals bit length minus 1, plus popcount.
